title: The work list
dek: What is being done here, as opposed to what is known.
lead: Every other register on this site answers what is *known* — [what has been read](/searched/), the [open questions](/open-questions/), [what cannot be closed](/gaps/), the [errands](/errands/) and the [corrections](/corrections/). None of them answered **what is being done**, so that lived in a chat window, which is the one place that does not survive the session. This is that list, in the shape the whole estate keeps it in. An item here names **who has to move it**, because an item with no owner is how a list becomes wallpaper.
close: Nothing is struck from this page when it turns out to be wrong; it is struck **through**, the same way a retracted claim is treated in [corrections](/corrections/). A list that quietly deletes its mistakes is telling you only what it wanted to be true.

rows.what: Read the regiment's book by hand — retired, not performed
rows.note: **Retired by the control rather than carried out, and the distinction is deliberate.** Images 652–662 were read (December 1787 to July 1791, no Llerena). Images 663–950 were **never read and now will not be**: the book is in the full-text index and Sancho is absent from it under all three spellings. *Done* is the nearest of the five states to what actually happened — the question this row existed to answer is answered, by cheaper means. **The caveat survives**: machine transcription of eighteenth-century hands is imperfect, so an index absence is weaker than a page absence, and if anything later contradicts this the 290 images are still there.

rows.what: Run the Berroeta control before reading another 290 images
rows.note: **Run and passed, 15 September 2026.** «Capellán del Regimiento Infantería de Buenos Ayres» returns **22 results** from a collection titled *Montevideo. Military Award Records 1812–1814*, with snippets reading «…de Berroeta Capellán del Regimiento…» and years **1789, 1790, 1791, 1792** — the chaplain and the exact years of the book. **The regiment's book is in the full-text index**, so the absence of any military collection from the 68 results for «Sancho Llerena» is evidence rather than a gap in coverage. Two limits kept open below.

rows.what: Finish harvesting the 68 full-text results for «Sancho Llerena»
rows.note: The sweep of 15 September returned **68 results** against far fewer in this archive's earlier attempts, and only about fifty titles and **three** snippets were actually read before the block returned. Results 51–68 were never displayed at all. Re-run at 100 per page, extract every ark, and resolve each through the tile service's manifest to a film and image — that route keeps working while the main site is blocked.

rows.what: Open two collections found in that sweep — both opened
rows.note: **Both opened.** *Montevideo Catedral, Baptism Records 1825–1828* at **dgs:007713376 images 515 and 601** — Francisco Juan Ramón (22 March 1826) and Lucinda Gregoria del Corazón de Jesús (12 May 1827), both grandchildren of Sancho through Dominga. *Cordón, Religious Marriage Records 1825–1916* at **dgs:007713391 image 1669** — Justa Pastora's marriage of 3 November 1830. **All three acts turned out to be already held**, which is what made the parent-pair query a coverage check rather than a discovery.

rows.what: Read DGS 7713375 — the Montevideo cathedral baptisms
rows.note: A film this archive had never named until 15 September. It holds the **1789 godparent act at image 551** and the **1811 baptism of Luis at image 2410** — the best document there is on Sancho's parents. Two images of it have been read and nothing else. It spans at least 1785 to 1811, which is the whole of Sancho's Montevideo life.

rows.what: Settle the Sánchez question — settled, against this session's own objection
rows.note: **Read at magnification: the castrense man is *"Manuel Sánchez, Sargento de 1ª Clase del Regimiento, natural de la Ciudad de Córdova"*.** The Canelones petitioner is *"natural del Reino de Andalucía"*. **They do not match.** A man from the Andalusian city would be called *of Andalucía* — what the Canelones clerk writes, and what Sancho's own act means by *Córdova la Llana* — while an unqualified *la Ciudad de Córdova* in a Montevideo register most naturally means **Córdoba del Tucumán**, named in full a few leaves earlier in the same book. **So the objection this session raised against its own argument is withdrawn**, with the caveat that removing a counter-example is not producing evidence.

rows.what: Find the real Montevideo index, 1726–1800
rows.note: **DGS 7713386 is not it.** This archive called it «Índices de bautismos, matrimonios y defunciones, 1726–1800» and called opening it *the cheapest test in the archive*; images 300 and 1500 are cathedral burial registers of **1887 and 1905**. Two samples of 2,244 do not prove the index absent from that film, but the attribution is disproved and is logged in [corrections](/corrections/). The index may exist under another DGS — find it the way the Canelones one was found, from an image's own Information panel rather than from a catalogue line.

rows.what: Open a Córdoba parish register — the next country
rows.note: «Córdova la Llana» is the **city of Córdoba** in Andalusia; no municipality of that name exists because it is an epithet, and the qualifier distinguishes it from Córdoba del Tucumán. So Sancho was born there about 1767 and his parents **Félix Llerena and Rosalía Aguilar were natives of the same city**. **Nobody has yet looked at a single Córdoba parish register.** That is now the largest unopened door in this archive, and it is in Spain rather than Uruguay.

rows.what: Resolve Anton Armando Lerena — two records, deliberately not merged
rows.note: **Resolved 15 September 2026, and there was never a contradiction.** The J193 says Anton Armando Lerena died **3 April 2003**; estate 15127/2013 was advertised on **page 68** of the gazette of 16 August 2013. This archive's row held the **gazette year** and the **page number**, and this session read them as a death year and an age. gendatabase was right. One man. Logged in [corrections](/corrections/), along with the discovery that the whole column was mislabelled.

rows.what: Buy one South African death notice
rows.note: The 1994 death notice of **Ricardo Juan Carlos Lerena** (b. 1920, m. 1941 Doreen May Chappell) from gendatabase.com — the source David found, which this archive had never tried. A South African death notice **names the deceased's parents**, which would put in a modern official document what this archive currently infers: that the Cape Lerenas descend from Pablo Armando. **This session does not create accounts and does not pay for things**, so it stops here. Logged in [errands](/errands/).

rows.what: Settle whether five deaths in 1999 are a catastrophe or an artefact
rows.note: Five of the fifteen gendatabase death rows carry **1999** — Catherine Tertia Karon, Gayle Lerena, Pierre Frederick Lerena, and two children aged eight and thirteen, including a married couple. Either something terrible happened to this family in 1999 or the index has a default-year artefact, and **a summary row cannot tell you which**. Needs the actual death notices, which are behind the same paywall. Nothing of it is published as fact in the meantime.

rows.what: Give the estate the film-and-image addressing method
rows.note: **Written up in `notes/FOR-THE-ESTATE.md`, 15 September 2026**, where a sibling session will find it, with working code and the traps spelled out. Covers `dgs:{film9}.{film9}_{image5}`, the `manifest.json` ark round-trip, **why it matters — the tile host is not behind the Error 15 block that takes down `/search/` and `ark:` pages together** — and `tools/fsimage.js` with its three traps.

rows.what: Two catalogue attributions in this archive were wrong — the estate should assume its own are too
rows.note: **Written up in `notes/FOR-THE-ESTATE.md`, 15 September 2026**, where a sibling session will find it, with working code and the traps spelled out. Both cases set out in full: **7713373**, where the label was wrong and the substance held, and **7713386**, which is simply not the index it was called. Plus the film-gap lesson — three probes are not a survey — and the one-call `manifest.json` test that settles any of it.

rows.what: Invent a register of outstanding work for this archive
rows.note: **Founded on a mistake and kept rather than deleted.** On 15 September this session was asked whether outstanding work was tracked centrally, found that it was not, and wrote `data/open-threads.tsv` — **the ninth session to invent its own answer**, which is precisely how this estate acquired a `Chip` meaning two things and one chart drawn under three names. The right thing already existed in the kit, written first in the Defranceschi archive. The content of that file has been folded into this list and the file retired. The lesson is the one the kit's own check states: a convention that lives in a document drifts, because nothing is checking it.

rows.what: Find Sancho Llerena's marriage act
rows.note: **Found 15 September 2026** after the archive had spent weeks recording it as probably not digitised. DGS 8166578, **image 2687** — «En ocho días del Mes de Enero de **1791** años… Sancho Llerena, natural de Córdova la Llana, hijo legítimo de **Félix Llerena** y de **Rosalía Aguilar**, naturales de dicha Córdova… con **María Fernández**, natural de las Asturias, hija legítima de **Rodrigo Fernández**». The year is in arabic numerals. It settles Córdoba against Granada, corroborates Apolant's date, confirms his parents independently of the 1811 baptism, and corrects the trees on the bride's father.

rows.what: Walk the Canelones informaciones matrimoniales
rows.note: **Finished 15 September 2026, with a negative.** DGS 8166573 does not cover January 1791: Volumen 6 runs to November 1790 and ends at image 1459, Volumen 7 opens at 1460 and its first dated case is March 1791. Sancho married on 8 January. The whole of 1791 in that series is one expediente belonging to somebody else. **A seam in the filing, not a failed search** — and the caveat is recorded: the filming card reads «hojas sueltas», so a stray sheet could sit elsewhere in Volumen 7. It also produced the one hard fact about the man himself: at image 2167 he is sworn as a witness and **could not sign his name**.

rows.what: Decide whether gendatabase-derived facts may stay on a public site
rows.note: **Materially reduced, 15 September 2026.** David chose to re-source rather than argue fair citation, and the South African Government Gazette — free and official — carried more than the index did. **The three sons of the 1950 estate are now off the commercial source entirely**: Ricardo Juan Carlos with exact dates, Nuno Fernando with exact dates and a wife nobody knew of, Rogue Luis Armando with his identity number. What is **still gendatabase's alone** is the later generation — Doreen May, Roberto Juan Roque, Brigitte Zaage, Anton Armando, Patricia MacEwan, Jeanette Riekstins, Belinda Michael, Paul Raymond, Rhena May, and the five deaths of 1999. Their gazette notices exist and are located but unread, so the decision is narrower than it was but not gone. **The attribution has still not been stripped.**

rows.what: Close the two limits on the Berroeta control
rows.note: **Both closed, 15 September 2026.** *Limit one:* six arks from the 22 results were resolved through the tile service's manifest — **five return DGS 7713373**, images 657, 667, 676, 716 and 831, and **image 657 is a page this session had already read by hand**. So the collection labelled *Military Award Records 1812–1814* is the regiment's book, whatever its label says. The sixth returns **DGS 7713382 image 2736**, the Montevideo marriage register. *Limit two:* all three spellings swept — «Sancho Llerena» 68, «Sancho Lerena» 143, «Sancho Lorena» — and **not one hit comes from DGS 7713373**.

rows.what: Finish the gazette re-sourcing — five estate notices already located
rows.note: **Four of the five done, and the fifth is a real null.** Read off the gazette: Anton Armando (b. 1952, d. 3 April 2003), Roberto Juan Roque (b. 20 March 1944, d. 20 February 2022), Brigitte (b. 16 October 1951, d. 18 May 2023), Belinda Maud (b. 16 January 1957, d. 2024 — the printed day is impossible and is flagged, not smoothed), and **Rogue Luis Armando in full: born 6 December 1905, died 29 January 1973**, which makes him the eldest of the three sons by fifteen years. **Doreen May could not be re-sourced**: her estate number returns only two J187s, neither carrying a date. Still open and moved to its own row. Also still unchased: the 1986 notice for **Lerena Racing Stables**, which belongs on [the horses page](/horses/).

rows.what: Find Doreen May Lerena's J193, and put Lerena Racing Stables on the horses page
rows.note: Two leftovers from the gazette work. **Doreen May** is the only person in this family who could not be taken off the commercial index: estate **16409/00** returns two J187 accounts and no J193, so gendatabase's *born 1921, died 1999* stands as **their** fact. Her notice may sit in an unindexed or badly scanned gazette of **2000**. And the **1986 notice for Lerena Racing Stables** (Government Gazette, 8 August 1986, no. 10383, page 7) has been located and never opened — it belongs beside the gazette's own description of Robert Paul Lerena as a **racehorse trainer**.

rows.what: Map what is filmed and indexed for Córdoba and Asturias — done, and it changed the plan
rows.note: **Answered 15 September 2026, and the answer is two-sided.** *The bad half:* **Córdoba's parish registers are not on FamilySearch.** The Research Wiki's Church Records section for the province lists no FamilySearch collection at all — the registers are with the **Diocese of Córdoba**. Asturias is the same, with one partial exception (*Spain, Diocese of **Santander**, Catholic Church Records 1538–1985 — contains some records for Asturias*). Full text for Andalusia is nobility and notarial only. So Sancho's baptism is **not** sitting on a film waiting to be addressed by number; **that route is a letter to a diocesan archive, not a search**. *The good half, which corrects this session's own pessimism:* the provincial wiki pages are not the whole picture. A record search for Llerena in Spain 1730–1800 returns **228 results** from national collections the Córdoba page never mentions — *Spain, Catholic Church Records 1307–2005*; *Spain, Baptisms 1502–1940*; *Spain, Marriages 1565–1950*; and **Spain, Granada, Catholic Pre-Marriage Investigation Files, 1556–1899** — the same record type walked at Canelones this morning, indexed, for Andalusia, in the right century. **The eighteenth century is reachable by index even where it is not reachable by image.**

rows.what: Find Sancho Llerena's baptism, Córdoba, about 1767
rows.note: The single most valuable document not yet looked for. The act of 1791 puts his birth in the **city of Córdoba**; the trees say **about 1767** and that is still only a tree. A baptism would give the date, the parish, and his grandparents — **a fifth generation**, where this archive currently stops at four. Note the act gives no age, so 1767 is unverified and the search window should be generous, say 1760–1775.

rows.what: Find the marriage of Félix Llerena and Rosalía Aguilar, Córdoba, 1750s–60s
rows.note: The 1791 act says both were **naturales de dicha Córdova**, which is the first evidence placing the generation above Sancho anywhere at all. Their marriage act would give **their** parents and their own birthplaces. One tree claims Félix was born about 1725 and married about 1753, every value "about" and none sourced — treat it as a search hint, not a fact.

rows.what: Search Asturias for Rodrigo Fernández and Rosa Fernández
rows.note: **Never searched, in any form.** Two independent parish acts name them — the 1791 marriage and the 1811 baptism of their grandson Luis — and both say **naturales de las Asturias**. The 1791 act adds that they were **vecinos de Santa Lucía** in Uruguay, and the 1812 padrón puts Rodrigo, 63, *asturiano*, living in Sancho's own household. So they emigrated and lived with the family: their Asturian parish is findable and would carry María Fernández's baptism too.

rows.what: Test the Llerena–Aguilar compound in Spanish records — run, and it argues against hidalguía
rows.note: **Run 15 September 2026.** «Llerena y de Rosalía Aguilar» returns **zero**; «Félix Llerena» returns only modern Latin America; «Rosalía Aguilar» returns forty collections of which **two** are in Spain, both Jaén notarial of 1829–37. On its own that would be worthless — **so the control was run first.** The corpus that *is* indexed for Andalusia is **nobility and hidalguía files, chivalric orders and Madrid protocols**, searchable back to 1489 — exactly where an armigerous couple would appear. They do not. **Weak evidence that Félix and Rosalía were not gentry with a Chancillería file**, which sits with the 1811 act calling Sancho *Don* while the 1798 deposition says he could not write his name.

rows.what: Find Sancho Llerena's death
rows.note: **Searched 15 September 2026; a controlled null.** No indexed death or burial exists for him in Uruguay under any spelling — across 401 loose results he appears only as *father*, *father of the bride*, *spouse* or *other*, **never as the principal of a death**. **The control passed**: a surname-Rodríguez search for Montevideo deaths 1828–1838 returns church burials from **Nuestra Señora del Carmen, Cordón** — the exact parish where Justa Pastora married in 1830 and where Dominga lived — dated 1832, 1833 and 1838. So burials in his family's own parish, in the decade he is supposed to have died, **are** indexed, and he is not among them. **What that does not mean**: the index is name-based and a mangled surname is invisible to it, and the Cordón is one parish of several. He is not in the index; that is not the same as not in the registers. **The trees' 1832 remains a tree.**

rows.what: Find María Fernández's death
rows.note: **Same search, same control, same result.** No indexed death or burial for María Fernández, wife of Sancho Llerena, in Uruguay 1810–1870. She returns only in records already held. **One gain**: FamilySearch's index gives her *Parents Rosa Fernández, Rodrigo Fernández* — **a third independent witness** to what the 1811 baptism and the 1791 marriage act both say. Three sources, one couple, no disagreement.

rows.what: Build the complete list of Sancho and María's children from the registers
rows.note: The archive has them piecemeal — Pedro Antonio 1793, Agustina Ramona 1795, Fidel about 1799, Justa Pastora 1800, José Loreto 1806, Luis 1811 and others — assembled from scattered searches rather than from a systematic read. **Canelones baptisms 1791–1815 are filmed and the images are now addressable.** Reading them straight through would produce a closed sibling list instead of an open one, and the consistency checker already reports that its sibling tests reach only 106 of 277 people.

rows.what: Take Pedro Antonio Lerena forward from 1793
rows.note: **Traced.** His marriage was already held — **Vicenta Vega, *natural de Cerro Largo*, daughter of Don Romualdo and Doña Andrea Maestre** — but **his children were not**: the indexes give **Manuel Antonio** and **Vicenta Margarita**, and a **Pedro Antonio Natalio baptised at the Cordón on 12 December 1828**, born 1 December. One entry names his mother as **María Fernández**, consistent with him being Sancho's son; another garbles his father as *Francisco Llorena*, which is why these are recorded as candidates and not attached to the line.

rows.what: Read the 1812 padrón from the image, not from a transcript
rows.note: The archive quotes it — Sancho, *andaluz*, 45; María Fernández, 36; Rodrigo Fernández, 63, *asturiano*, in the household — but from a published transcription. Now that images are addressable by number, **read the entry itself**: padrones often carry occupation, household composition and enslaved people in columns transcriptions drop. Sancho's age of 45 in 1812 implies birth about 1767, which is currently the only support for that year.

rows.what: Reclaim the errands that are now machine work — and the premise was wrong
rows.note: **The row assumed eleven errands sat on David. They did not — all eleven were already owned by *me*, this archive.** That is the third time today this session asserted something about its own files without checking them. **But it exposed a real fault underneath**: by the estate's own division — *errands.tsv is work for a person, the work list is work for a session* — eleven rows of the archive's own machine work were sitting in the wrong register. **All eleven migrated**: closed in `errands.tsv` with their detail kept verbatim, and seven new work-list rows opened for the ones that had no counterpart. What remains in errands is what it should be — institutions written to, and four things genuinely waiting on David. **Postscript: the migration was too blunt and `drift.py` refused it.** Setting all eleven to *done* claimed work was finished because its index entry had moved — and one of them says in its own detail that the register **has never been turned**. All eleven are back at *ready*, each now carrying a pointer to the work list, which is where their state is maintained. **The checker was right and the migration was wrong.**

rows.what: Find the DGS for the Montevideo marriage-dispensation register, 1856–1932
rows.note: Logged as an errand for David when catalogue search was returning *Something Went Wrong* all day. The route that works now: open any image from the right parish and read its **Information panel**, which prints the catalogue link and that reel's item-by-item contents. The archive already holds one dispensation from this series — the 1911 Lerena–Cardozo — so an anchor exists.

rows.what: Search the Iglesia del Cordón, Montevideo
rows.note: Full text has already shown this archive two Cordón collections it has never opened — **Baptism Records 1828–1836** and **Religious Marriage Records 1825–1916**. The Cordón is where the Montevideo branch surfaces in the 1830s, and the 1831 Rivera godfather act sits there. Fold the errand into that work rather than leaving it addressed to David.

rows.what: Place Catherine Mary Sophia Lerena, born 25 March 1929
rows.note: **A wholly new person, produced this afternoon by the gazette**: the surviving spouse of Nuno Fernando Lerena, who died 1 July 1971 at 24 Leiden Road, Gerdview, Germiston. Nobody in this archive knew he was married. Her identity number is partly legible in the notice; her own estate, if she has one, would be findable on gazettes.africa and would name children — **grandchildren of Pablo Armando nobody has counted**.

rows.what: Ask where Rogue Luis Armando was born in 1905
rows.note: Directly tests one of this archive's declared [gaps](/gaps/) — *the eight years between Northam and the Cape*. Pablo Armando was born at Rosario in **1882**; his eldest son was born **6 December 1905**. If that birth was not in South Africa it locates the family in those missing years, and **Argentina is the obvious first place to look** — the archive already has Argentine baptism sweeps to extend.

rows.what: Find out who Rose Lilian Theys was
rows.note: The 1950 estate makes her **Executrix Testamentary**, gives her **a half-share of the residue**, and describes her as **"no relation"** — while listing her address as **No. 7 Forth Road, Newlands**, the same address as the deceased. A woman who is not a relative, lives with him, administers his estate and inherits a quarter of it is not a minor figure. gazettes.africa and the deceased-estates index will both carry her.

rows.what: Sweep gazettes.africa for TAYLOR and BOOYZEN
rows.note: The gazette pipeline works and cost nothing; it has so far been pointed only at *Lerena*. The other two South African lines in this archive are **Mary Septima Taylor**, Pablo Armando's wife, and the **Booyzens** who appear in the DNA as Cape Afrikaners. Estate notices would give both families exact dates and surviving spouses. **Search surname-first** — modern notices print *LERENA, Anton Armando*, not the other way round.

rows.what: Pull the Rapeport Incorporated thread
rows.note: One firm at **107 Oxford Road, Rosebank** acted for Doreen May in 2001, Anton Armando in 2013, Roberto Juan Roque in 2022 and Belinda Maud in 2024 — **a quarter-century of one family's estates**. That is not a coincidence and it is a way of establishing which Lerenas belong to this family without guesswork. It is also a live firm, which makes it a David question rather than a search, if it comes to contact.

rows.what: Make the build catch a stale errand
rows.note: **Done — `tools/check-errands.py`, wired into `verify.sh`.** It fails the build when an errand whose status is still open carries a detail that announces the errand is finished. **It found a false positive on its very first run** — an errand saying the work *"cannot be closed online at all"*, which is about feasibility, not about the errand — so the patterns were tightened to phrases that can only mean *this errand is over*. A bare *closed* is useless here, and **a noisy check gets switched off**. Then proved both ways: planting the real case (the 1791 marriage errand set back to *ready*) makes it exit 1 and name the row; restoring it returns to green. **40 errands checked, none finished-but-open.**

rows.what: Audit this archive's other catalogue-derived film numbers
rows.note: Distinct from the estate-wide warning below it. **Two of two Montevideo attributions failed inspection today** — DGS 7713373 was mislabelled but right, DGS 7713386 was simply wrong. Every other DGS in this archive that came from reading a catalogue rather than opening the film is now suspect. They are cheap to test: one `manifest.json` call resolves any image to its true film and image number.

rows.what: Check the living-person gate — the tick was assumed, and now it is asked
rows.note: **Audited, and the suspicion was right.** `checkliving.py` finds living people from an explicit flag — `living`, `presumedLiving`, `alive`, `isLiving`, or `conf: "living"`. **`people.json` carries none of them**, so the green tick was passing over an empty set. The kit's own docstring says that is *"correct rather than a gap"* **for an archive that genuinely has no living people** — which had never been established here. **So it was established.** Of 278 people, three are born 1930 or later with no death recorded: Rieta Maria (1936) and Antoinette Septima Lynette (1943) are both **over eighty and presumed deceased** by the rule the checker itself applies; **Anton Lerena, born 1952, was not** — and he is the one person the archive was publishing who might have been alive. **He is not**: the J193 read today gives his death as **3 April 2003**, which also upgrades him from *named in the tree, not corroborated by a document*. **The gate now passes over a set that has been counted.**

rows.what: Warn the estate that pdftotext will weld two strangers together
rows.note: **Written up in `notes/FOR-THE-ESTATE.md`, 15 September 2026**, where a sibling session will find it, with working code and the traps spelled out. With the actual welded line quoted, how it was caught — two gazettes disagreeing about one estate number — and the whole free pipeline, including the predictable `archive.gazettes.africa` slug.

rows.note: **Written up in `notes/FOR-THE-ESTATE.md`, 15 September 2026**, where a sibling session will find it, with working code and the traps spelled out. With both worked examples: **died 1994, filed 1996** and **died 2003, filed 2013** — the second of which cost this archive several hours believing two records described two men.

rows.what: Decided: this session does not create accounts or pay for sources
rows.note: **A standing constraint, recorded as a decision rather than left implicit.** gendatabase.com's full records, and the South African death notices behind them, sit behind a subscription. This session does not sign up and does not pay. The consequence is visible and deliberate: **Doreen May Lerena is the one person in this family who could not be taken off a commercial index**, and her dates remain that source's rather than this archive's. The alternative — re-sourcing from the free official gazette — was tried first and worked for everyone else.

rows.what: Decided: no routing around the FamilySearch block
rows.note: **Also standing.** FamilySearch's security layer blocked this session repeatedly today. The archive does not switch browsers, use another network, or otherwise get around it. The consequences are accepted and written down instead: the Berroeta control waited hours, the variant sweeps are still unrun, and **every zero returned by a blocked page was discarded rather than recorded as a null** — which is the rule that matters, because a blocked page and an empty result look identical.

rows.what: Decided: not reading 290 more images until the control is closed
rows.note: Row 1 was *running* this morning and is now parked. **Reading the regiment's book by hand was the right plan only while nobody knew whether it was indexed** — the Berroeta control showed that it is, in one search, and a day of work evaporated. Kept rather than deleted because machine transcription of eighteenth-century hands is imperfect, so **an index absence is weaker than a page absence** and the hand-read may yet be needed if the two limits in row 18 do not close cleanly.

rows.what: Open Canelones Baptism Records 1776–1794 — a volume nobody here knew existed
rows.note: **Opened 15 September 2026.** It is **DGS 8166573, images 72–478** — the same film as the informaciones, in a separate block, and **this archive already held an ark into it** without ever resolving it. Pedro Antonio's baptism is at **image 274** and has now been read from the image rather than a transcript: **"Pedro Antonio de la SS.ma Trinidad"**, born 31 July 1793, godparents **Don Antonio Alemán and his wife**. Opening it also disproved this session's own claim that the film held nothing below image 1057 — see [corrections](/corrections/).

rows.what: Open Montevideo Catedral Religious Marriage Records 1782–1797
rows.note: A Montevideo marriage register covering 1791, never opened here, surfaced while resolving the Berroeta hits. Sancho married at Canelones, so this is not where his act is — but it is where the marriages of **his comrades, his witnesses and his wife's Asturian family** would be, and **DGS 7713382 is now anchored at image 2736**, which is a way in.

rows.what: Open the three later Montevideo cathedral baptism volumes
rows.note: **1811–1813, 1831–1833 and 1840–1842**, all carrying hits under one spelling or another, none opened. They cover the generation after Sancho — the years when this family moves from Canelones into Montevideo and when Luis, Fidel and Pedro Antonio are raising children. The 1811 volume also brackets the baptism of Luis this archive already holds, at DGS 7713375 image 2410.

rows.what: Identify P. R. Lerena of Lerena Racing Stables, Randburg
rows.note: The 1951 gazette calls **Robert Paul Lerena a racehorse trainer at Newlands**; a 1986 gazette lists **P. R. Lerena Racing Stables, P.O. Box 425, Randburg** as an employer. Establish it from documents, and note that this family's racing connection may run to living people, who stay out of this archive.

rows.what: Read the three images the parent-pair query found — all three were already held
rows.note: **Read, and the row's own premise was wrong.** All three are acts this archive already had: **Dominga Josefa's baptism of 15 May 1804** (godparents Joseph Ponteceli and Agueda Rivero), **Francisco Juan Ramón, 22 March 1826**, and **Lucinda Gregoria del Corazón de Jesús, 12 May 1827** — the last two in fuller words here than the index gives, with the Capitán, the Mayor Don Joaquín Ruiz de Carvallo and a General as godfather. Logged in [corrections](/corrections/).

rows.what: Run the parent-pair query on every couple in the register
rows.note: **A method, not a lookup, and it generalises.** Searching two parents as one phrase only matches when a document names both — so it finds children, children's marriages and grandchildren in one query, and it does not drown in the 190,000 results that the surname alone returns. Worth running for **Félix Llerena and Rosalía Aguilar** in Spain, for **Rodrigo and Rosa Fernández** in Asturias, and for every couple in the register where the consistency checker currently reports no reachable siblings.

rows.what: Re-open the 1754 Granada marriage — chased, unreadable, and the lead deflated
rows.note: **Two results, both negative, and the second is the useful one.** *First:* the expediente has its own record (**ark 1:1:XPG2-RYP**) and it is **Image Unavailable**, with no image ark exposed and a **completely empty** collection wiki page — so no film number can be recovered and the film-and-image trick has nothing to bite on. Its index entry is **thinner** than the marriage index already held. *Second:* this session's own lead was an over-read. The 1754 bride **Ana María de Aguilar is of La Malá — La Malahá, in Granada province**, which this archive had already recorded; **our Rosalía Aguilar is of Córdoba**. Only the groom is Cordoban, and *Aguilar* is among the commonest surnames in Andalusia. An earlier session had already run the decisive test — a structured search for a son *Sancho de Lerena y Aguilar*, returning a controlled **No Results Found** — and **was right to close the file**. Logged in [corrections](/corrections/).

rows.what: Search the Granada pre-marriage files for Félix and Rosalía — a controlled null
rows.note: **Searched, and the answer is a real absence — after two fake ones were thrown away.** Exact-surname queries returned zero twice, and **both were discarded**: the same exact-match shape cannot retrieve the 1754 act that is *known* to be in that collection, because the indexed surname is the compound *Lerena y Armenta*. A null from a query that cannot find what is there is not a null. The working shape — non-exact surname, exact given names, Spain, 1735–1785 — **passes its control**, returning the Granada Pre-Marriage collection and the full 1754 record for the known couple. Run for **Félix Llerena and Rosalía Aguilar** it returns 305 results and **not one Andalusian collection** — nothing from Granada, Córdoba, Sevilla, Jaén or Málaga. **Their marriage is not indexed by FamilySearch anywhere in Andalusia in the fifty years that must contain it.** With Córdoba's parish registers not filmed either, the searchable routes are closed and what remains is the diocesan letter. **The 1791 act stays the only document this archive has that names them.**

rows.what: Write to the Diocese of Córdoba — the parish registers are only there
rows.note: The mapping row above establishes that **Córdoba's parish registers are not digitised by FamilySearch**. The originals are at the **Archivo General del Obispado de Córdoba**. What is wanted is narrow and citable: the **baptism of Sancho Llerena, about 1767**, son of **Félix Llerena and Rosalía Aguilar**; and their **marriage**, about 1750–1766. Both parents are stated *naturales de dicha Córdova* on the Canelones marriage act of 8 January 1791, which is the citation to quote. **Left to David because it is correspondence with an institution**, and because the shared note both archives keep says to search the sent mail before writing to any archive.

rows.what: Walk the Cordón burial register by image, 1826–1845
rows.note: **The route the null leaves open.** Sancho and María are absent from the burial *index*, but the index is name-based and an eighteenth-century surname mangled by a transcriber is invisible to it. **Nuestra Señora del Carmen, Cordón** is the family's own parish — Justa Pastora married there in 1830, the 1831 godfather act is there, Dominga lived there — and its burials of 1832–38 are demonstrably filmed. The Cordón marriage register is already anchored at **dgs:007713391 image 1669**, so the burial volume is findable from the same reel's item boards. Do the Iglesia Matriz next, and Santa Lucía after that, where María's parents were *vecinos*.

rows.what: Walk the Iglesia Matriz burial register, 1826–1845
rows.note: The Cordón is one parish of several and Sancho may not be in it. The **Catedral de la Inmaculada Concepción** — the Iglesia Matriz — is where he stood godfather in 1789 and where his son Luis was baptised in 1811, so it is at least as likely a resting place. Its baptism films are already anchored (**DGS 7713375**, images 551 and 2410), which is the way into the same reel's burial volumes.

rows.what: Walk the Canelones burial register, 1826–1845
rows.note: The third candidate parish, and the one where he married, where five of his children were baptised and where he swore his 1798 deposition. **DGS 8166573 is already mapped** — images 72–478 are the baptisms and 1057–3295 the informaciones — so the burial volume is likely on a neighbouring reel of the same diocesan filming, findable from the item boards.

rows.what: Search Santa Lucía — his wife's family were vecinos there
rows.note: The 1791 marriage act says **Rodrigo and Rosa Fernández were vecinos de Santa Lucía**. A couple often ends up buried where the wife's people are, and this archive has never opened a Santa Lucía register of any kind. It is also where **María Fernández** herself may be, and she is missing on the same terms.

rows.what: Test whether the Guerra Grande broke the registers
rows.note: **Tested, and they did not.** Montevideo church burials are indexed continuously across the period: **1832, 1833, 1838** in the first window, **33 indexed burials for one surname in 1839–1848** including 1841 and 1842, and **1852** in the next — all from *Uruguay, Catholic Church Records* at **Nuestra Señora del Carmen, Cordón** and Montevideo. The siege of 1843–51 did not destroy them. **So Sancho's absence from the burial index is not explained by register loss**, which strengthens the negative and justifies walking the images. *One honest limit*: indexing density is not the same as register survival — the 1850s window returns 7 where the 1840s returns 33, and that could be thinner indexing rather than fewer burials.

rows.what: Establish the last date Sancho is attested ALIVE
rows.note: **Done, and it corrects this session twice over.** Fourteen records name him; only **four** require him to have been standing there — godfather in **1789**, sworn witness in **1798**, padrino at the **1804** confirmations, and enumerated in the **1812 padrón** at calle San Juan No 60, household 59, as *Sancho, andaluz, 45*. **A census enumerates the living, so 1812 is the last document in the world that shows him alive** — not 1798, as this row itself claimed when it was written. Everything after is father, grandfather or ancestor, up to 1850, and **a dead man can be all three**. So the unaccounted gap before the trees' 1832 is **twenty years**. Written up in `data/sancho-last-alive.tsv`; the misstatement is in [corrections](/corrections/).

rows.what: Find Pablo Armando's arrival in South Africa

THAT IS FALSE, and it was pointing the search the wrong way. *** The card's *Oficina enroladora* reads *** CAPETOWN ***, with *Región Militar* and *Distrito Militar* both blank — *** which is the signature of a man registering at his own CONSULATE because he was already abroad. *** Far from placing him in Argentina, *** the card is evidence he had already left it. *** And the 1908 date is itself unsourced: the card carries no year but the class of 1882, sits in a collection catalogued 1911–1936, and the passport's page 6 gives a Cape Town consular *libreta* of **1915**. See /enrolment-card/.

rows.what: Draw the two lines on the home page — done, at David's request

rows.what: Fix /bloodline/ — nobody is drawn twice, and nobody is their own brother
rows.note: **Raised by David, 16 September 2026**, looking at Nuno Fernando's chart: *"2 juan carlos lerena's and 2 mario lerenas and mary septima twice."* Two faults, both in the kit's drawing rather than in this archive's data. **First**, a husband or wife was always drawn as a chip beside the person, with no check that they were already on the chart in their own right — and every married pair of ancestors is two blood relatives, so each got a box AND a chip of the other. *** 13 relatives came out in 22 boxes *** A chip is now drawn only for somebody the chart does not already hold; where both halves are on it, they are seated together and the marriage is a tie between them. **The test is the slug, never the name.** **Second**, the register deliberately keeps a row for the mangled machine-index reading of Pablo Armando, so the false trail stays visible — and the sibling pass handed that row its own person as a brother. An alias now folds onto the person it is a spelling of. Fixed in the kit (`bloodline.js`, `bloodline.client.js`, commits `7f776b3` and `45b37a7`) and in `tools/build-people.py`; kit repinned. Checked against all six archives that draw this chart: the graph is byte-identical for five, and Lerena loses exactly the one alias.

rows.what: The other five archives need repinning to pick up the /bloodline/ fix

rows.what: Read the DNA matches properly, at both companies

rows.what: Run the maternal aunt's chart against the granddaughter's — done, and it found one

rows.what: Piedmont: mapped in detail, and the Turin route cannot close it — the Argentine end can
rows.note: *** Opened 16 September 2026 out of David's question, "do we have a Juan Carlos Lerena / Lerina in Italian records?" *** *** The direct answer is no *** — no Giovanni Carlo or Gian Carlo under either spelling, controlled. *** The useful answer is that LERENA and LERINA are Italian surnames and they sit in PIEDMONT: *** 66 exact Lerena records in Italy clustered in the **Diocese of Torino**, and **114** exact Lerina, Torino again plus **Ivrea**. See `data/italy-lerena-lerina.tsv`. *** And that is the same corner the DNA points at. *** The archive's own DNA page reasons that Cheryl's **11.1% Italian**, with three non-Italian grandparents, implies **about 44% in Pablo Armando — one Italian parent** — and that the split is *** NORTHERN-dominant, 6.1 against 3.6. *** *** Two independent things, an admixture estimate and a surname distribution, now point at northern Italy, and neither of them names anybody. *** *** WHAT TO DO WITH IT: *** the Torino and Ivrea civil registration and diocesan records are indexed on FamilySearch and are searchable by parent name — *** so look for a LERINA or LERENA male born about 1840–1862 in Piedmont who then DISAPPEARS from the Italian record ***, and cross him against the Argentine arrivals. The archive already holds `cemla-lerina.tsv`: a **Lerina family of four landing at Buenos Aires from GENOVA on 15 March 1889** — *** seven years too late to be his parents arriving, but the right surname on the right route ***, and Genova is the port Piedmont emigrates through. *** Also worth re-running CEMLA for LERENA and LERINA before 1882, which is the arrival that would matter. *** *** ANTENATI CHECKED, 16 September 2026, and it cannot answer this. *** The Italian State Archives' own portal returns **one** Lerena in its whole national name index — *** Cesare Lerena, death 1915, BRESCIA *** — and eight Lerina, most of them the different surname *Di Lerina*. *** The control destroys that null: *** Antenati holds **2,621 registers for Torino**, but a name search there for ROSSI restricted to Torino returns 102 people called *** Charles, Marguerite and Jacinte, in 1805–1811 *** — *** the Torino name index is NAPOLEONIC ONLY, kept in French, and does not reach the 1840s–1880s at all. *** *** So Antenati's images exist for Piedmont and are not name-searchable for the years that matter *** — the same lesson as the Rosario typescript and the FreeREG Devon parishes, that the null belongs to the finding aid and not to the past. *** The searchable collection for the right years is FamilySearch's "Italy, Torino, Torino, Civil Registration (Tribunale), 1866-1899" ***, which is where the 66 and 114 came from. Antenati's 2,621 Torino registers are the fallback: browsable by comune and year, image by image, the way Rosario and Canelones were read. *** WORKED IN DETAIL 16 September 2026, and the conclusion is negative in a useful way. *** **49 Lerina records in and around Torino** — Ivrea, Montaldo Roero, Costigliole — *** families that stay put for sixty years ***, with two Carlo Lerinas acting as fathers and neither a candidate for anything. *** THE ROUTE IS STRUCTURALLY INCAPABLE of answering the question: *** the Turin civil series begins in **1866**, so a man born in the 1840s–50s has no birth record in it at all; and *** an emigrant leaves no later Italian record by construction ***, so "a son who vanishes" cannot be told from an unindexed death or a move. *** Enumerating Piedmontese Lerinas maps the people who STAYED, which is the complement of what is wanted. *** *** Do not spend a week on it. ***

rows.note: *** REWRITTEN the same day it was opened, because the control demoted half of it. *** *** THE STRONG HALF STANDS: there was no LERENA and no LERINA household, under any spelling, anywhere in SANTA FE PROVINCE in the 1895 National Census. *** Controlled: a Gonzalez search returns **88,739** records with the 1895 census reaching San Cristóbal, **Alberdi/Rosario**, San Jerónimo and Iriondo, so the index is dense and covers Rosario itself. *** For a whole surname to be absent from a province indexed that thickly, it has to be genuinely absent *** — and that agrees with the Rosario baptism sweep from an entirely different record type. *** THE WEAK HALF IS WITHDRAWN AS EVIDENCE. *** This archive said earlier today that Pablo Armando's own absence from the 1895 census at thirteen suggested he had already left. *** It suggests nothing of the kind. *** One person can always be missed or mangled, and *** this person's name demonstrably mangles: the Argentine army indexed his own card as "ARMAND LORENA", born "Rosario de Lerma, SALTA". *** A boy who becomes Armand Lorena on one index can be anything on another. *** SO THE HONEST POSITION IS THAT NOTHING DATES HIS DEPARTURE: *** born Rosario February 1882, son born Cape Town November 1905, *** twenty-three years with no record inside them. *** The live routes are the ones hypothesis 2 already names — *** UK outward passenger lists (BT 27), indexed from 1890 *** — and the consular file behind the 1940 passport. *** And note the archive already reasoned that the South African War shipped some 360,000 horses in, Argentina among the sources, when he was 17 to 20 and a horseman. ***
